outcome: As far as the sources I could read show, no finite octal game has been newly shown to have an eventually periodic nim-sequence since 26 January 2024, and the universal claim is still stated as open (Wikipedia, last revised 11 March 2026; Flammenkamp's table, updated 11 October 2026). But Nowakowski's 2025 unsolved-problems column (Games of No Chance 6) says 'significant progress' has been made on A2, and I could not read what that progress is, so an in-window advance on this problem is not excluded.
problem_asks: (1) A universal claim over every finite octal game: every octal game whose octal code has finitely many nonzero digits (digits 0 to 7; examples in the sources: ·45, ·137 (Dawson's chess), ·007 (Treblecross), 4.777). (2) For each such game, the nim-sequence G(0), G(1), G(2), ..., the nim-value of a heap of each size n. (3) That nim-sequence is eventually periodic: from some point on it repeats with a fixed period, so a preperiod and a period exist, both finite. The statement is one yes/no universal question. It asks for no bound on the period or preperiod, no count of exceptions, and it names no particular game. A yes answer needs (1), (2) and (3) to hold for every finite code. The statement does not restrict to impartial or normal-play games in words, but the sources all mean impartial normal-play octal games.

events.what_happened: Waldmann (2002) characterises eventual periodicity of an octal game's Grundy sequence: it is eventually periodic if and only if it has only finitely many nonempty Grundy languages, all regular. Stated as Theorem 3 (Waldmann, 2002) in the 2019 arXiv paper 1902.07011 (search snippet; neither the 2002 paper nor 1902.07011 was opened).
events.delivers: A reformulation, not a resolution: it turns eventual periodicity into a regular-language condition for each game. It settles no specific game and no class by itself.
events.remains: Every instance of the universal claim: the characterisation must still be checked game by game.
events.doubts: Known only through a restatement in a later paper, not the original.
events.direction: Neutral: a reformulation of the question for each game.

events.what_happened: Horrocks and Nowakowski, 'Regularity in the G-sequences of Octal games with a Pass', Integers 3 (2003), article G01. Per a search snippet: received 19 Sep 2002, revised 27 Mar 2003, accepted 7 Apr 2003, published 9 Apr 2003. It shows that adding a single pass move to one heap allows arithmetic periodicity, and it notes that finite octal games are not arithmetic periodic (attributed to Austin). The PDF did not read through WebFetch.
events.delivers: Arithmetic periodicity for games with a pass move (a different game class and a different property). Per the snippet, it says nothing settles whether the G-sequence of a finite octal game is periodic.
events.remains: The whole universal claim (periodicity, not arithmetic periodicity, for games without a pass).

checked_by.what_they_did: published the paper (accepted 7 April 2003 per a search snippet)

events.doubts: Read only via search snippets; the arithmetic-periodicity claim is per the snippet.
events.direction: Neutral to the periodicity question; it is about a different property in a different game class.

events.what_happened: Dailly, Duchêne, Larsson and Paris, 'Partition games', arXiv:1803.02621 (v1 7 March 2018; v2 24 October 2019; v3 15 May 2020), Discrete Applied Mathematics 285 (2020) 509–525. The abstract shows that several partition-game rulesets (CUT) have periodic or arithmetic periodic Sprague-Grundy sequences, for infinite classes and by a computational test. It frames the work against take-and-break games such as octal and hexadecimal games and describes a 'break-without-take' subclass.
events.delivers: Periodicity for some partition-game rulesets (heaps split into parts from a set). These are not the finite octal games of this problem: the rulesets are a different class, framed against octal games. Settles no octal code.
events.remains: The whole universal claim for finite octal games.

checked_by.what_they_did: published the paper in volume 285 (2020), pp. 509-525

events.direction: Neutral: periodicity for a different class of games.

events.what_happened: Songsuwan, 'Node-Kayles on Trees', arXiv:2512.24221 (December 2025 batch; exact day not read). Per a search snippet, Theorem 1.1 states that the Grundy-value sequence of a family of grafted rooted trees in Node-Kayles is eventually periodic, and the same paper re-derives preperiod 51 and period 34 for Node-Kayles on paths (which is the octal game ·137, Dawson's chess). The period-34 result for ·137 is attributed in search snippets to Guy and Smith (1956), so this is a re-confirmation, not a new octal result. Not opened.
events.delivers: Eventual periodicity for a family of graph games (grafted trees), a different class from the finite octal games. Its ·137 case restates a result from 1956 (per a snippet), so it settles nothing new for this problem.
events.remains: The whole universal claim for finite octal games.
events.doubts: Read only via a search snippet; the claimed theorem is per the snippet and I did not check the paper.
events.direction: Neutral for the universal claim: a periodicity result for a different graph-game class.

events.what_happened: Michael Fisher, Keith Hazen and Craig Tennenhouse, 'Olympic Games: Three Impartial Games with Infinite Octal Codes', Integers 24 (2024), G3 (received 10 Feb 2024, accepted 4 Oct 2024, published 25 Oct 2024; per a search snippet, the PDF did not read through WebFetch). The paper computes the P-positions of three octal games whose codes are infinite, built from Beatty sequences for the golden, silver and bronze means. Fisher had given a talk on it at Bryn Mawr and Haverford in September 2023, described as an undergraduate project; I found no earlier written version.

Per the introduction (search snippet), it reports that among the nontrivial finite octal games with at most three digits, 14 are solved and 63 unsolved, which conflicts with the Bielefeld table's 20 (see disputes). It proves nothing about finite octal games.

events.delivers: A weak solution for Inverse Treblecross (an avoidance variant, not a finite octal game). It does not decide the periodicity of ·007 or of any octal game.
events.remains: Periodicity of ·007 and the whole universal claim.
events.doubts: The Sprague-Grundy pattern stated by the third-party review site is unverified. The acknowledgements, read only in a search snippet, thank a person for computations to n ≤ 50.
events.direction: Neutral: a different (avoidance) game.

events.what_happened: Kai Liang, 'A Finite Automaton Approach to Combinatorial Games', arXiv:2608.13273 (v1 13 Aug 2026, v2 29 Aug 2026). Per its abstract: finite automata are built for games whose positions are regular languages, then formally verified; it introduces a generalized misère quotient for partizan octal games, reports solving most two-digit partizan octal games and many misère cases, proposes a partizan version of Guy's conjecture, and claims periodicity of outcomes and Sprague-Grundy values for Kotzig's nim under normal and misère play.
events.delivers: Partizan octal games (not impartial) under normal and misère play, and Kotzig's nim, which is not an octal game. It does not claim periodicity for impartial finite octal games, so it does not settle the problem's class. Its partizan results are not the problem's question.
events.remains: The impartial finite octal question, which the abstract does not address. The paper's own open problems (per a search summary of the Nowakowski–Ottaway search, not read) concern algebraic periodicity of partizan octal games.

machine_checked.system: automaton construction with formal verification (system named only as 'rigorous formal verification' in the abstract)

events.doubts: The full text did not read (PDF binary, HTML not available), so the verification's scope, and whether it uses any AI tool, are unchecked. The abstract's claim of solving Kotzig's nim periodicity is not checked.
events.direction: Neutral for the impartial question: partizan octal games and Kotzig's nim.

events.what_happened: Kai Liang, 'Infinite Subtraction Games with Periodic Outcomes and Aperiodic SG Values', arXiv:2608.17654 (v1 18 Aug 2026; v2 1 Sep 2026). The abstract says the paper finds special cases of subtraction games with infinite subtraction sets whose outcome sequences are periodic while their SG-value sequences are bounded and aperiodic, and it gives examples. Section 2 quotes an open question (attributed to Nowakowski's list) about an infinite subtraction set with periodic outcome sequence and aperiodic nim-sequence, and says 'These are easy to find in octal games.' A revised note at the top of the paper (August 2026) states that the previous version 'claimed to solve an open problem', that the problem had already been resolved in Lomič's work, which the author's literature review had missed, and that the preprint 'will not be submitted for journal publication'.
events.revisions: v1 18 Aug 2026 (claimed to solve an open problem); v2 1 Sep 2026 with a revised note (August 2026) withdrawing the novelty claim.
events.delivers: Examples of infinite subtraction games with periodic outcomes and aperiodic bounded SG values. These are not finite octal games. The novelty claim is withdrawn by the author in the revised note, which credits Lomič's prior work.
events.remains: Whatever the paper does not address. It does not address finite octal games on its face.
events.doubts: The sentence 'These are easy to find in octal games' is ambiguous on the class of octal games. If it means finite-code octal games, it would bear directly on the problem and would cut against the conjecture. Read in context it probably concerns infinite-code octal games, but Section 2 was only partly readable, so this is not established.

withdrawn.what: The author's claim (v1) to solve an open problem on infinite subtraction games, withdrawn by the revised note: the problem had been resolved in Lomič's work; the preprint is an additional example in Lomič's framework and will not be submitted to a journal.

events.direction: Neutral on the universal claim as stated; possibly cuts against it if 'octal games' in Section 2 means finite-code octal games (not established).

events.what_happened: Danai, Ellis and Thanatipanonda, 'Two Dimensional Subtraction -- Transfer Games', arXiv:2602.14325 (February 2026), per a search summary: generalises Lengyel's periodicity results for two-pile subtraction-transfer games and shows that nim-values of a large class are periodic, with exact periods in many cases. Not opened; only the search summary and a review site were seen.
events.delivers: Periodicity for a class of two-pile games with subtraction and transfer moves. These are not finite octal games (they have two piles and transfer moves), so they settle nothing for this problem.
events.remains: The whole universal claim for finite octal games.
events.doubts: Read only via a search summary.
events.direction: Neutral: periodicity for a different game class.

Not opened.
events.delivers: Periodicity for a variant of subtraction games (sink convention, additive sets). It is not stated to be a finite octal game, so it settles nothing for the problem on its face.
events.remains: The whole universal claim for finite octal games.
events.doubts: Read only via a search summary.
events.direction: Neutral: periodicity for a subtraction-game variant.

events.what_happened: Larsson and Manabe, 'additive subtraction games' (March 2026), per a search summary: determine the full nim-value structure of additive subtraction games in the primitive quadratic regime, building on a problem from Winning Ways. Arxiv ID 2603.10414 (v2 cited). Not opened.
events.delivers: Full nim-value structure for a class of additive subtraction games in one regime. It is a subtraction-game class; whether any of its games are finite octal games is not stated in what I read. Settles no finite octal game on its face.
events.remains: The whole universal claim for finite octal games.
events.doubts: Read only via a search summary.
events.direction: Neutral: full analysis of a subtraction-game class.

disputes.summary: Counts of the nontrivial games and solved games disagree. Wikipedia (last revised 11 March 2026): 167 inequivalent octal games with at most 3 digits; 79 (with leading 0) and 14 (leading 4) repeat within 250 terms; only 20 of the rest solved. Bielefeld table (updated 11 October 2026): 93 nontrivial games (period plus preperiod above 250), and 20 solved rows, though its text says nineteen. Integers 24 (2024) G3 introduction, per a search snippet: 79 nontrivial games with at most three digits, 14 solved, 63 unsolved. Bielefeld's separate unsettled list has 11 codes marked as unknown sparse-space structure, a different property. GitHub 'SolvedGames' lists nine games; GitHub 'UnsolvedGames' lists 83 codes. These categories are not reconciled here.

Year of the Gangolli–Plambeck solutions: Bielefeld gives October 1988 for ·16, ·56, ·127, ·376; GitHub gives 1989. The talk note is archived with a 22 October 1988 date; the journal publication is 1989 (per a snippet). Year of ·354: Bielefeld gives October 2012; GitHub gives 2002.
Preperiod of ·454: 160949018 in Guy's survey (search snippet) against 160949019 in arXiv 1803.02621 (search snippet). Not reconciled.

Who conjectured the periodicity: the 1988 Plambeck talk attributes it to R. Guy ('It is conjectured [R. Guy]'); a search snippet of the 2024 Integers paper attributes it to Berlekamp, Conway and Guy, and Wikipedia attributes the listing of it as an open problem to Guy. Who introduced octal games: one snippet credits Smith, another Guy, with Guy–Smith joint work as the usual reference. Not resolved here.

The Liang preprint 2608.17654 claimed to solve an open problem on infinite subtraction games (v1, 18 Aug 2026); its revised note says Lomič's earlier work had resolved it. Lomič's paper was not located. This is a withdrawn priority claim on a neighbouring class, not on finite octal games.

summary: The problem asks whether every finite octal game (octal code with finitely many nonzero digits) has an eventually periodic nim-sequence. I ran 45 web searches and opened about 16 pages, including Wikipedia's Octal game article, the Plambeck–Gangolli talk note on Eppstein's page, Flammenkamp's Bielefeld table and its unsettled list, OEIS A395248, the GitHub repository tczajka/octal-games (raw SolvedGames and UnsolvedGames), the arXiv abstracts 2608.13273, 2604.16759, 1803.02621 and 2608.17654 (HTML v2, including its revised note), and the Cambridge chapter page for GONC6. The primary PDFs of the Nowakowski columns (GONC4, GONC5, GONC6), the Integers 2024 G3 paper, the 2003 Horrocks–Nowakowski paper and the 2019 Waldmann restatement came back as binary, 404 or 503, so what I say about them comes from search snippets and is marked opened: false. On the readable sources, the universal claim is still open. No finite octal game has been newly settled since 26 January 2024: the latest dated solution in Flammenkamp's table is from October 2012, the table was updated on 11 October 2026, and Wikipedia (last revised 11 March 2026) still lists the claim as open. In-window events are the 2024 Integers paper on infinite-code octal games (outside the class), the 2025 GONC6 column, the 2026 OEIS computation for ·007 (values to 2^30, periodicity unknown, so no proof), and 2026 papers on partizan octal games, Inverse Treblecross, infinite and additive subtraction games and two-pile games, none on finite impartial octal games. Two in-window items could change this. First, the GONC6 column (online 18 May 2025) says 'significant progress in the older problems can be found in A1, A2, A5, B1, C1, C2, and E7'. I could not read the A2 entry, so I do not know whether the progress is per game, per class or general. If it is a general result, the record's outcome changes; if per game, it moves no universal quantity. Second, Liang's 2608.17654 says, of a phenomenon with infinite subtraction sets, that 'these are easy to find in octal games', quoting Nowakowski's list. Read literally for finite octal games, this would cut against the conjecture. In context (infinite subtraction sets; the 2024 paper's own focus on infinite codes) it most likely means infinite-code octal games, but Section 2 was only partly readable, so I have not resolved it. The same preprint's revised note withdraws its novelty claim: the problem was already resolved in Lomič's work, which I could not locate. That withdrawal concerns subtraction games with infinite subtraction sets, so it is recorded as a neighbour. Per-game events from 1956 to 2012 are individual solutions: ·45, ·156, ·356, ·644, ·165, ·055, ·16, ·56, ·127, ·376, ·454, ·104, ·106, ·054, ·354, 4.064, 4.344, 4.364, 4.404 and 4.406. Each settles one instance of a universal claim and, per the scope rule in §2.1, moves no quantity the problem names, so I recorded them as events and did not treat them as progress on the universal claim. A class-level point should be recorded: finite subtraction games, whose digits are only 0 and 1, are a subclass of finite octal games, and their eventual periodicity has been known since Golomb (1966). Per a 2026 snippet and Nowakowski's list, that class is settled, but it does not settle the universal claim. Counts disagree across sources (Wikipedia 20 solved; the Bielefeld table 20 rows with dates; the Integers 2024 paper's 14 solved and 63 unsolved; GitHub nine solved and 83 unsolved codes). They are recorded as disputes and not reconciled, since none changes the universal status. AI involvement: no AI system is named in any source I read about this problem, so none_found is true where I read the source and null where I could not read the text (the GONC6 A2 entry, the Integers 2024 G3 text, the full text of 2608.13273, the 2003 pass paper, the Node-Kayles preprint). I searched for AI involvement with octal and nim terms and GPT, Claude, Gemini, AI model, LLM, AlphaEvolve, FunSearch, Erdős-problem trackers and 2026 lab announcements. The lab results I checked by secondary coverage are OpenAI's Astra (1 August 2026; ten results, none on impartial games), DeepMind's AlphaProof Nexus (May 2026; nine Erdős problems, no game identified), OpenAI's unit-distance disproof (May 2026) and Claude Opus 4.6 on Knuth's problem (February 2026); none concerns octal or nim games. I read none of the lab primary sources (Astra's manuscript, the AlphaProof Nexus preprint) and did not open the Tao Erdős-problem tracker, so the AI search is negative within the sources I could reach, not exhaustive.
competing_reading: The strongest case for an in-window change is that the GONC6 column's 'significant progress' on A2 is a general result or a complete class analysis, which would make the record's outcome 'an event moves the problem' rather than 'nothing new'. The strongest case for treating the Liang sentence as a counterexample is the literal reading that 'octal games' means finite octal games, under which aperiodic SG values would occur in the problem's own class; I think the infinite-subtraction context and the 2024 paper's infinite-code focus make that unlikely, but Section 2 was only partly readable. The strongest case against counting the per-game solutions at all is the scope rule: each is a finite instance of a universal claim and moves no quantity the statement names. The strongest case for counting them is that the problem's status is worked out from events, so their dates and instance-level content are the evidence the later pass needs.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The A2 entry in Nowakowski's 'Unsolved problems in combinatorial games' (Games of No Chance 6, pp. 55–98, DOI 10.1017/9781009565486.005): what the 'significant progress' on A2 is and which games or classes it covers. (2) Section 2 of arXiv 2608.17654 in full, to see whether 'octal games' there means finite-code octal games and which list it quotes. (3) The Integers 24 (2024) G3 paper's introduction and results, to check its count of 14 solved and whether it states anything about finite octal games. (4) The Lomič subtraction-games paper, to identify what it resolved and whether it touches finite octal games. (5) The current Flammenkamp solved and unsettled pages with their dates, to confirm that no finite octal game has been added since 2012, and to resolve the 2002/2012 date conflict for ·354. (6) The Guy and Smith 1956 paper, and Gangolli and Plambeck's 1989 note, to check the attributions and periods given here from listings.
